title: Numerical derivation 1: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 1)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. The derivations in this module therefore always begin by naming the class, then applying the class-specific integral or sum, then checking the result against the defining property.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 1)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: E = integral |x(t)|^2 dt ; P = lim (1/T) integral |x|^2 ; x_e = (x(t)+x(-t))/2. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 1 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Numerical derivation 1: Systems & LTI Properties — worked from first principles (parameter set 1)

A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. title: Numerical derivation 1: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 1)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

title: Numerical derivation 1: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 1)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. Difference equations become rational H(z) by term-by-term transformation, and inverse transforms are checked by power-series expansion so that algebra and sequence agree coefficient by coefficient.

Discrete-time spectra are periodic with period 2 pi, finite data produce the DFT's N bins, and sampling replicates spectra every fs so that overlap becomes aliasing. title: Theoretical derivation 9: Systems & LTI Properties — worked from first principles (parameter set 9)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. Equality for all inputs proves the property; a single counterexample disproves it, which is why each derivation ends with an explicit verdict and the boundary case that would change it.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Theoretical derivation, parameter set 9)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: T{a x1 + b x2} = a T{x1} + b T{x2} ; delayed input must give delayed output. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Communication channels are governed by two complementary laws. Shannon's capacity, built from bandwidth and SNR, is an upper bound no coding can exceed in noise; Nyquist's formula turns a chosen rate into required signal levels on a noiseless channel. Derivations here convert decibels carefully, compute capacities with every logarithm shown, and then chain the two laws in the engineering order: Shannon first for feasibility, a practical rate below it, Nyquist last for levels and baud, finishing with attenuation and SNR bookkeeping in dB.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Theoretical derivation, parameter set 9)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: C = B log2(1+SNR) ; BitRate = 2B log2(L) ; dB = 10 log10(P2/P1). Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 9 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Theoretical derivation 9: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 9)

title: Numerical derivation 10: Systems & LTI Properties — worked from first principles (parameter set 10)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. Equality for all inputs proves the property; a single counterexample disproves it, which is why each derivation ends with an explicit verdict and the boundary case that would change it.

title: Numerical derivation 16: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 16)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 16)

title: Numerical derivation 19: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 19)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Discrete-time spectra are periodic with period 2 pi, finite data produce the DFT's N bins, and sampling replicates spectra every fs so that overlap becomes aliasing. title: Formal proof-style derivation 32: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 32)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. title: Theoretical derivation 33: Modulation & Transmission — worked from first principles (parameter set 33)

title: Theoretical derivation 36: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 36)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. title: Theoretical derivation 39: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 39)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. Difference equations become rational H(z) by term-by-term transformation, and inverse transforms are checked by power-series expansion so that algebra and sequence agree coefficient by coefficient.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Theoretical derivation, parameter set 39)

title: Formal proof-style derivation 41: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 41)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. title: Formal proof-style derivation 47: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 47)

title: Formal proof-style derivation 56: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 56)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. title: Theoretical derivation 60: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 60)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. Difference equations become rational H(z) by term-by-term transformation, and inverse transforms are checked by power-series expansion so that algebra and sequence agree coefficient by coefficient.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Theoretical derivation, parameter set 60)

title: Formal proof-style derivation 62: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 62)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. title: Theoretical derivation 63: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 63)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. title: Numerical derivation 70: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 70)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Communication channels are governed by two complementary laws. title: Numerical derivation 73: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 73)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. Modulation moves information onto a carrier by varying amplitude, frequency or phase, and digital keying quantises that variation into constellation points. These derivations expand AM products into carrier and sideband terms with power accounted watt by watt, apply bandwidth rules (double-sideband, Carson for FM) with their assumptions stated, and convert between baud and bit rate through bits per symbol, always returning to the constellation picture where distance between points explains noise immunity better than any slogan.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 74)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: s_AM = Ac[1+mu m(t)] cos(wc t) ; BW_AM = 2 BWm ; BitRate = Baud x log2(L). Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 74 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. title: Formal proof-style derivation 77: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 77)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 77)

title: Theoretical derivation 78: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 78)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. title: Formal proof-style derivation 83: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 83)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Discrete-time spectra are periodic with period 2 pi, finite data produce the DFT's N bins, and sampling replicates spectra every fs so that overlap becomes aliasing. The derivations in this module pass carefully between DFS, DTFT and DFT instead of conflating them, evaluate small DFTs directly from the definition sum, and treat the sampling theorem as a geometric statement about spectral copies: recovery is possible exactly when the copies do not overlap, and the anti-alias filter is what enforces that precondition.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Theoretical derivation, parameter set 87)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: X(e^{jW}) = sum x[n] e^{-jWn} ; X[k] = sum_{n<N} x[n] e^{-j2pikn/N} ; fs >= 2 fm. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 87 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Theoretical derivation 87: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 87)

title: Theoretical derivation 87: Modulation & Transmission — worked from first principles (parameter set 87)

title: Theoretical derivation 87: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 87)

Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics.
